---
title: "Get started with mcplite"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(mcplite)
```

This article shows the complete first-use workflow and the authoring details
needed for schemas, rich results, protocol compatibility, and safe deployment.

## 1. Install mcplite

Install the released version from CRAN:

```{r install-cran, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("mcplite")
```

Install the development version from GitHub:

```{r install-github, eval = FALSE}
pak::pak("tosidata/mcplite")
```

## 2. Save a complete server script

Save the following as `server.R`. It defines one inventory tool and then starts
the server.

```{r complete-server, eval = FALSE}
library(mcplite)

inventory_status <- tool(
  function(item) {
    stock <- c(apples = 12L, coffee = 0L, tea = 5L)

    if (!item %in% names(stock)) {
      stop("`item` must be apples, coffee, or tea.", call. = FALSE)
    }

    list(
      item = item,
      count = unname(stock[[item]])
    )
  },
  name = "inventory_status",
  description = "Report the local inventory count for a known item.",
  arguments = list(
    item = type_enum(
      c("apples", "coffee", "tea"),
      "Item whose inventory should be checked."
    )
  )
)

mcp_server(list(inventory_status))
```

A tool combines an R function with a client-facing name, description, and
argument schema.

`mcp_server()` blocks the R process while it serves requests. Put it at the end
of a client-launched script, after all tools have been defined or sourced.

## 3. Configure the client

Add a server entry to your MCP client's configuration. The `command` must
resolve to the `Rscript` executable. GUI-launched clients may not inherit your
shell's search path; if `Rscript` is not discoverable, run
`Sys.which("Rscript")` in R and use the returned absolute path as the client's
`command`. Replace the server path below with the absolute path to the
`server.R` file you saved. The script path must be absolute because the
client's working directory is not guaranteed.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "r-inventory": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": [
        "--vanilla",
        "/absolute/path/to/server.R"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Configuration file names and locations vary by client; use the client's MCP
server configuration instructions.

## 4. Restart the client and use the tool

Restart the client so it launches the new server. The client should then list
`inventory_status` as an available tool. Ask it to check the local inventory for
coffee. Success means the result identifies `coffee` with a count of `0`; exact
presentation varies by client.

The client and server communicate over standard input and output. The server
exits when standard input closes.

## Return ordinary R values

Ordinary R return values are the simplest default. A character scalar becomes
literal text, character vectors are joined with newlines, and other
JSON-serializable values, such as the named list returned by
`inventory_status`, become JSON in a text content block. Ordinary `NULL` becomes
the text `"{}"`; an ordinary `list()` becomes `"[]"`. Bare lists are ordinary
values, not MCP result objects.

For per-tool serialization choices, return your own JSON as ordinary character
text, for example with `as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(value, na = "null"))`.
`mcplite` does not parse JSON-looking text or insert it as raw JSON.

## Build structured and rich results

Use `tool_result()` for structured content, explicit MCP content blocks, result
metadata, or a tool-level error. For example:

```{r structured-result, eval = FALSE}
tool_result(
  content = content_text("Found two matches."),
  structured_content = list(
    matches = c("tea-green", "tea-black")
  ),
  meta = list(source = "local inventory")
)
```

If `structured_content` is supplied without `content`, `tool_result()` generates
one JSON text fallback block. Explicit content is preserved without an extra
fallback. `NULL` omits structured content; a bare empty list at the structured
root represents `{}`. Nested unnamed empty lists retain jsonlite's `[]`
mapping. With default options, these R values have distinct structured-content
meanings:

| R value | Structured-content meaning |
|---|---|
| `list(ok = TRUE)` | JSON object |
| `c("a", "b")` | JSON array |
| `"done"` | JSON string scalar, not parsed as JSON |
| `list()` or `structure(list(), names = character())` | Empty JSON object `{}` |
| `I(list())` | Explicit empty JSON array `[]` |
| `NA` or `NA_character_` | JSON `null` |
| `NA_integer_`, `NA_real_`, or `NA_complex_` | JSON string `"NA"` |
| `NULL` | No structured-content field |

JSON-looking strings and jsonlite `json` objects supplied as structured content
remain string values. See `tool_result()` for details of R-to-JSON mappings.

Image, audio, and resource blob constructors accept data that is already
base64-encoded; they do not read files, download URLs, infer MIME types, or
encode payloads. Resource links carry an author-supplied URI but do not add a
resource endpoint to the server.

## Choose payload JSON mappings

Configure these package-global R options near the top of the server script,
before constructing results and calling `mcp_server()`. Keep them stable while
the server runs.

| Option | Default | Supported choices |
|---|---|---|
| `mcplite.json.null` | `"null"` | `"null"` or `"list"`: encode named payload `NULL` fields as `null` or `{}`; fields remain present |
| `mcplite.json.na` | Unset | Omit jsonlite's `na` argument, or select `"null"` or `"string"` |
| `mcplite.json.auto_unbox` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` or `FALSE`: automatically unbox singleton payload vectors or keep them as arrays |

Defaults preserve jsonlite's class-specific missing-value mappings. Selecting
`na = "null"` also maps `NaN` and infinities to JSON `null` and retains missing
data-frame fields. Disabling automatic unboxing changes singleton values such
as `count = 1L` to `[1]`; explicit `I()` and `jsonlite::unbox()` representations
still apply. This standalone example inspects the generated text without
starting a server and restores the session's options afterward:

```{r payload-options}
local({
  old <- options(mcplite.json.na = "null", mcplite.json.auto_unbox = FALSE)
  on.exit(options(old))
  result <- tool_result(structured_content = list(
    count = 1L,
    values = c(NA_real_, NaN, Inf, -Inf),
    rows = data.frame(id = 1L, missing = NA_real_)
  ))
  cat(result$content[[1]]$text, "\n")
})
```

Remove any option with `NULL`, for example `options(mcplite.json.na = NULL)`,
to restore its default. Removing that option omits `na` rather than forwarding
`na = NULL` to jsonlite.

The options affect ordinary noncharacter return-value JSON and structured
content, including representability checks, generated fallback, and version
projection. They never change protocol fields, schemas, annotations, or result
and content metadata. Tool authors remain responsible for conformance with
advertised output schemas.

## Report tool errors

An error raised by a tool, such as `stop("Unknown item")`, is contained and
returned to the client as a tool-level error. To report an expected domain
failure explicitly, return a result with `is_error = TRUE`:

```{r tool-error, eval = FALSE}
tool_result(
  content = content_text("The requested item is out of stock."),
  is_error = TRUE
)
```

## Describe input and output schemas

For common inputs, pass a named list of `type_*()` property helpers to
`arguments`. Incoming JSON arrays reach the tool function as R lists, not atomic
vectors. Schemas do not coerce or validate argument values or supply R defaults.
`required = FALSE` permits omission in the advertised schema; give the R
function a default for an argument that may be omitted.

This tool converts a numeric array with `unlist()` and defaults to a multiplier
of 1. The returned tool is still an R function, so you can call it directly:

```{r array-inputs}
sum_numbers <- tool(
  function(values, multiplier = 1) {
    sum(unlist(values, use.names = FALSE)) * multiplier
  },
  name = "sum_numbers",
  description = "Sum numeric values and apply an optional multiplier.",
  arguments = list(
    values = type_array(type_number()),
    multiplier = type_number(required = FALSE)
  )
)
sum_numbers(list(2, 3))
sum_numbers(list(2, 3), multiplier = 2)
```

`type_ignore()` omits an argument from the advertised schema. It does not reject
a caller-supplied argument or enforce permissions.

Use `type_from_schema()` when you need a complete input schema. The complete
schema must have direct root `type = "object"`; JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords such
as `$schema`, `$defs`, `$ref`, composition, and conditionals are preserved.

This tool uses a complete input schema and advertises an array-shaped structured
result:

```{r complete-schema, eval = FALSE}
search_items <- tool(
  function(query) {
    matches <- paste(query, c("alpha", "beta"), sep = "-")
    tool_result(structured_content = matches)
  },
  name = "search_items",
  description = "Find local items whose names start with a query.",
  arguments = type_from_schema(list(
    type = "object",
    properties = list(
      query = list(type = "string", minLength = 1)
    ),
    required = list("query"),
    additionalProperties = FALSE
  )),
  output_schema = type_from_schema(list(
    type = "array",
    items = list(type = "string")
  ))
)
```

## Protocol compatibility

`mcplite` supports modern MCP `2026-07-28` and legacy MCP `2024-11-05`,
`2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25` with the same server definition. The client
normally manages the lifecycle, but the distinction is useful when diagnosing a
connection:

- MCP `2026-07-28` selects the protocol on each request. `server/discover`,
  `tools/list`, and `tools/call` work without an `initialize` exchange.
- MCP `2024-11-05`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25` use an `initialize` exchange
  before tool operations.

Output schemas are projected according to the client's protocol:

- MCP `2026-07-28` receives supported object, array, scalar, and other schema
  shapes.
- MCP `2025-06-18` and `2025-11-25` receive direct object-root output schemas.
- MCP `2024-11-05` receives tool definitions without output schemas.

A tool is still available when its output schema cannot be represented by the
client's protocol. `mcplite` checks schema container shape and serializability;
tool functions own full schema validity, input validation, and output
conformance.

MCP `2026-07-28` can receive every supported JSON shape. MCP `2025-06-18` and
`2025-11-25` receive object-shaped structured content. MCP `2024-11-05` receives
content blocks without a structured-content field. Explicit or generated text
content therefore gives every supported client a useful representation.

Text, images, embedded resources, annotations, and result metadata work across
all supported versions. Audio, resource links, and per-content metadata are
available with MCP `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`, and `2026-07-28`. A
`2024-11-05` call that returns audio or a resource link receives a contained
tool-level error instead of terminating the server.

## Use ellmer tools

Compatible `ellmer::tool()` definitions can be supplied directly to
`mcp_server()`. `ellmer` is optional; tools created with `mcplite::tool()` do not
require it.

## Configure tracing

Tracing requires the optional `otelsdk` package and uses standard `otel` and
`otelsdk` configuration. To send traces from an existing server script to stderr:

```sh
OTEL_R_TRACES_EXPORTER=stderr Rscript --vanilla /absolute/path/to/server.R
```

Never send telemetry to stdout because stdout is reserved for MCP protocol
traffic. Use stderr or a remote exporter instead. See `mcp_server()` under
"OpenTelemetry tracing" for configuration and propagation details.

## Server scope

`mcplite` is designed for local, client-launched stdio tool servers. It does not
provide HTTP transports, prompt or resource endpoints, subscriptions,
cancellation, sampling, elicitation, roots, Tasks, MCP Apps, or server-initiated
and other multi-round-trip feature families. Embedded resources and resource
links are result content, not resource endpoints.

## Trust and safety

Schemas describe inputs and outputs to clients; they are not authorization or
sandboxing. Each tool function is responsible for domain validation, permission
checks, credential handling, safe side effects, and appropriate output and
payload limits. Run the server with only the operating-system and data
permissions its tools need.

See the reference pages for `tool()`, `tool_result()`, `mcp_server()`, and the
`content_*()` and `type_*()` helpers for the full API.
